body:
I agree that this should be specified somewhere.

It seems like there will be many similar issues that need to be described - related to caret movement, text and non-text input, etc. .  I think it would make most sense to specify such details in a separate specification, maybe somewhat inspired by the [contentEditable spec](https://w3c.github.io/contentEditable/) which is about to be discontinued.

But if the maintainers of the HTML spec prefer to have it specified in the HTML spec, we can also do that. We should then probably come up with a proposal for a text in the Web Editing Working Group.

I don't have a strong opinion on where the behavior is defined. Though if it's not part of HTML, it should be clear from reading HTML where it is defined and what the boundary is between the documents. Some care will also have to be taken to allow for divergent platform behaviors, though I suspect that's not applicable to the case OP outlines.

cc @zcorpan

When I implement `plaintext-only` onto Firefox, I added some tests of that. https://wpt.fyi/results/editing/plaintext-only?label=experimental&label=master&aligned It seems that all browsers do nothing special in `plaintext-only`, i.e., the deletion work as same as `contenteditable=true` case. The tests in the directory checks only each browser's deletion work as same as when `contenteditable=true` and all browsers passed them. However, I guess there is no tests about deleting `` etc.

We discussed this in the previous Editing WG meeting. Currently, the behavior of `plaintext-only` is defined in `execCommand` in that some commands are disabled in that editing mode. The [`delete`](https://w3c.github.io/editing/docs/execCommand/#the-delete-command) and `forwardDelete` commands are not mentioned as being affected by `plaintext-only`, so have the same behavior as in `contenteditable=true`. This matches what browsers do.

Making it better defined what the effects are of pressing certain keys while an editable region is focused (or in general) seems like an issue for UI Events.

> Making it better defined what the effects are of pressing certain keys while an editable region is focused (or in general) seems like an issue for UI Events.

We were previously asked by the maintainers of the UI events spec to please not add more things into UI events. That's also why we now started a new spec initiative for this.

> Currently, the behavior of plaintext-only is defined in execCommand in that some commands are disabled in that editing mode. 

As of now, the `execCommand`spec has not reached FPWD and is full of descriptions of what browsers did one or two decades ago with a big disclaimer to please not use `execCommand`if at all avoidable.  In addition, `execCommand` has not been a central part of JavaScript-based editors for around 15 years now.

So this is not a good place to put this information.
UI Events can provide hooks for other specs to use.

> As of now, the `execCommand`spec has not reached FPWD 

That can be fixed.

> and is full of descriptions of what browsers did one or two decades ago

Yes, though they might not match reality exactly. Also, browsers haven't changed much in this area.

> with a big disclaimer to please not use `execCommand`if at all avoidable. In addition, `execCommand` has not been a central part of JavaScript-based editors for around 15 years now.

This is irrelevant.

> So this is not a good place to put this information.

I disagree.

> UI Events can provide hooks for other specs to use.

Yes, it may be a good idea to add a note into UI events somewhere referring to the new spec.

As for `execCommand`: I understand there are strong feelings involved every time possibly unshipping `execCommand` or closing down the unofficial draft spec comes up. I understand that some feel it is important to keep even if `execCommand` is no longer in (mainstream) use and it's not technically possible to reform `execCommand` in a way that would make it relevant because any JS-based dom modification will automatically break the undo history. 

So I don't think that is a good "can of worms" to open. On the other hand, I also don't think that adding more things to that document that are not directly related to the author-facing `execCommand` API is a good idea. That's also true for this.

Just to clarify: Yes, we agreed that deletions in `plaintext-only` should also delete non plaintext content based on common-sense consensus and unrelated to wording the unofficial `execCommand` draft spec.

> I understand there are strong feelings involved every time possibly unshipping execCommand or closing down the unofficial draft spec comes up.

Maybe feelings play into it, but the fact of the matter is that it's our job to describe the web platform, including the bits we might not like. `execCommand()` is very much part of the web platform.

> Maybe feelings play into it, but the fact of the matter is that it's our job to describe the web platform, including the bits we might not like. `execCommand()` is very much part of the web platform.

Sure. Let me try to rephrase. My point is that I don't think it's a good idea to ask all browsers to unship (most of) `execCommand` and close down the unofficial spec text even though it is no longer being used by mainstream JS developers, because there are feelings involved - probably on both sides - and the cause of that was before I started looking at this in 2014, so I don't really know the entire history of it.

The alternative is then to clean up the `execCommand` document and make it actually describe the author-facing `execCommand` API.  That is what I think should happen.

However, that does not mean that I think we should start using the `execCommand` document for other things, because it is currently a document that the mainstream JS developers who have moved beyond `execCommand` 15 years ago can currently ignore.

It is true that this unofficial draft spec contains some information about which of these commands should be ignored when used on content within a `plaintext-only` editing host. This was added in 2023 by @howard-e . I don't recall if we had a discussion about this addition in the Editing Working Group at the time, but even if we did, it only describes whether a command should be ignored if this API is used to execute one of these commands. It does not describe what happens upon user input. It's not given how these are mapped to one-another. 

For example, it could be argued that normal user input should not cause a deletion in a specific situation, but if the `execCommand` APi is used in the JS to call for a deletion, then it should still be executed. It could be assumed that end user input should be treated with reasonable default behavior but JS should be able to override this and cause other DOM changes. For that reason, I am actually not that certain that it's a good idea that `execCommand` was restricted in this way in 2023. On the other hand, given that we don't recommend the use of `execCommand`, it's also not that important how it is defined, it doesn't matter that much if it doesn't mean that we now start interpreting the `execCommand`-document to also define how contenteditable user interaction should work in general.
